Racisme anti-noir dans les écoles montré: Anti-Black racism in Montréal schools: “Sometimes it’s trivialized, sometimes it’s blatant”
Kemba Mitchell est consultante en racism: Kemba Mitchell is an anti-Black racism consultant. We put her findings up against the experiences of families who have been victims of discrimination.
Kemba Mitchell au cours d’une formation: Kemba Mitchell during an anti-Black racism training session at a Montréal elementary school. Courtesy of Kemba Mitchell.
La rentrée approche à grands pas ! Ce su: Back-to-school season is fast approaching! This subject probably doesn’t thrill every young person, but it leaves most vacationers the luxury of not having to worry about it. For others, however, school means anxiety, discrimination, humiliation, violence. And all for one reason: the colour of their skin.
J’ai donc voulu rencontrer plusieurs d’e: So I wanted to meet several of them to gather their stories. Listening to them, I felt like I was reliving my own experiences: being ignored when I raised my hand, being reprimanded more often by teachers, or being systematically considered at fault in conflicts because I was perceived as the “aggressive Black girl.”
Toutefois, en discutant avec Shana*, j’a: However, while talking with Shana*, I was deeply shaken by her story: my own experience seemed almost insignificant compared to what Leslie has endured. In 2024, that realization doesn’t reassure me. I thought the Equity, Diversity and Inclusion (EDI) approach had ensured that officers dedicated to these issues were deployed in every school in Quebec to enforce these principles. But to my great surprise, that’s not the case. “It’s a jungle,” one teacher told me.
Bien que les programmes de lutte contre: Although anti-racism programs look solid on paper, in reality they are almost absent from schools. Some schools even have to turn to anti-racist strategy consultants, a profession that is still uncommon but that, I hope, will become more common thanks to initiatives like this one.
<strong>Kemba Mitchell, consultante en r: Kemba Mitchell, an anti-Black racism consultant, has been offering workshops for teachers and students since 2020. La Converse met with this anti-racist strategy consultant, as well as a teacher, a student and a parent, to better understand why this work is needed.
À l’approche de la rentrée, certains sav: As the start of the school year approaches, some are savouring their last days of vacation, while others rush to get their school supplies ready. But for some students, Black students, anxiety is rising. School remains a place where they face discrimination.
Ces discriminations, Sarah*, une adolesc: Sarah*, a 17-year-old Black teenager with curly hair, has experienced all of this discrimination. A former student in the intermediate and minority education program, she recounts the following: “I wouldn’t say my teachers were openly or consciously racist, but with only 4 Black students out of 60 in my program, we felt a difference in treatment that came from certain prejudices,” she explains. Notably the prejudice that Black people are loud and disruptive. As soon as there was noise in the classroom, we were always the first to be pointed at by the teachers, as if we were the problem.
Les enseignants avaient tendance, ajoute: Teachers, she adds, tended to raise their voices more readily with Black students than with the rest of their classmates, whether they were white or racialized.
L’adolescente a attendu plusieurs années: The teenager waited several years before daring to raise the subject with the teachers concerned. And the response wasn’t what she had hoped for. “My feelings weren’t taken into account when I explained to my teachers that I perceived a difference in how they acted with me and with my classmates.” She continues: “When there were fights with other students, the white girls got off easily, while I faced much harsher penalties; they didn’t hesitate to exclude me quickly.”
<strong>Mépris des enseignants face aux: Teachers’ contempt in the face of racist violence between students
Shana*, maman de Leslie*, une fillette d: Shana*, mother of Leslie*, an 11-year-old girl, meets us at Place Ville Marie in the middle of summer. The sun is shining, flowers add colour to the city, but Shana’s face is marked by sadness as she shares her daughter’s story.
« On l’a poussée et violentée parce qu’e: “They pushed her around and were violent with her because she has Black skin,” she begins, nervously touching her wrist to contain her emotions. Leslie has just finished her last year of elementary school, in a school where she was in the minority. Despite a fresh start ahead in high school, the memory of that school year is a heavy burden for this pre-teen.
Shana poursuit, les larmes aux yeux : «: Shana continues, tears in her eyes: “The students would say things to her like: ‘You’re a monkey, go back home.’ They pushed her in front of everyone, it was humiliation, over and over again.” The mother tried to step in by contacting the school so that the situation would be looked into and the children responsible would be identified.
« Au début, le directeur m’a dit que l’é: “At first, the principal told me the school would take care of it, that he was sorry,” she explains. But the bullying didn’t stop. “Other students started saying horrible things, like ‘Go get yourself killed, you’re ugly.’ The insults got worse day after day, and the school did nothing. I called, I asked questions, but there was never any follow-up. It was total silence.”
Désespérée, la mère de Leslie finit par: Desperate, Leslie’s mother eventually filed a complaint with the Commission des droits de la personne et des droits de la jeunesse in February 2024. “It was too much. It was becoming dangerous for my daughter. She had even started tearing at her skin,” she says emotionally.
À ce jour, elle attend toujours la décis: To this day, she is still waiting for the Commission’s decision. Yet Shana believes the consequences of this harassment go beyond the walls of the school. She recalls the day she and her daughter were invited to a cooking activity at friends’ home. Leslie, seeing white children, refused to take off her coat despite the heat. “She was so afraid they would make fun of her skin, that they would call her dirty,” Shana says, her voice breaking.
« Elle nous a demandé : “Pourquoi les No: “She asked us: ‘Why do Black people go through all these atrocities?’” Shana says, catching her breath. “What I don’t understand is that we grew up in Ireland, surrounded by diversity. But here in Montréal, this everyday racism and the violence have marked her to the point that she now isolates herself and distrusts other kids,” she says, her eyes turned to the floor.
<strong>Combattre le racisme anti-noir s: Fighting anti-Black racism without talking about anti-racism?
C’est pour éviter que des enfants comme: It was to prevent children like Leslie and Sarah from suffering the same fate that Kemba Mitchell launched, in 2020, into anti-racist strategy consulting in schools.
« Le racisme anti-noir affecte de plusie: “Anti-Black racism affects our children at school in several ways: through the way teachers speak to them because of their implicit biases, through disproportionate suspensions and expulsions, and through the absence of role models in schools,” Kemba Mitchell begins. End-of-day traffic kept us from meeting her in person. So it’s on a screen that we discover her face: a radiant smile, underscored by a confidence you can feel.
Depuis 2008, l’approche Équité, diversit: Since 2008, the Equity, Diversity and Inclusion (EDI) approach has prompted a few reforms in the education system, notably by replacing the catechism and Protestant courses with the “Ethics and Religious Culture” course; the aim is to eradicate all forms of discrimination in schools through this course. But according to Kemba Mitchell, the change remains superficial, because it doesn’t allow the nature of racism to be fully addressed.
« Je n’interviens pas dans les écoles po: “I don’t go into schools to run EDI workshops. I tackle the problem head-on and focus more specifically on anti-Black racism,” the consultant continues.
Sa mission ? Montrer aux enseignants, pu: Her mission? To show teachers, and then students, how unconscious biases against Black communities are perpetuated in the school setting. To do this, the anti-racist strategy consultant uses case studies inspired by real events or fictional stories to help teachers and students become aware of their privileges.
« Dans mon travail, j’aborde la question: “In my work, I address the question of race by explaining its history, its construction in North America. When I explain that race was created to divide, to justify the enslavement of Africans and to legitimize colonization and the killing of Indigenous peoples, I also explain how today we are all victims of racism. Some of us are on the side of unjustified privilege, and some of us are not,” she sums up. “My goal isn’t to point the finger at teachers by telling them, ‘Yes, you, you’re racist!’ but rather to show the unconscious biases that some teachers may have.”
<strong>« J’ai lancé cette initiative po: “I launched this initiative to respond to needs I had observed”
Après 17 ans de soutien à la clientèle e: After 17 years in customer support and project management, Kemba Mitchell has seen her career take a new turn over the past four years. It was in 2020, when she applied for a community development officer position at the high school where Sarah studies, that Kemba realized how urgent it was to educate young and not-so-young people about anti-Black racism.
« Dans cette école secondaire, il n’y av: “In that high school, there was no Black authority figure except me,” Kemba continues. “So the simple fact that I was there allowed the few Black students who were there to feel safe and finally have some representation. They felt comfortable with me and opened up more easily about their experiences at school. I would then relay what they shared with me to the principal to make him understand there were steps to be taken.”
Durant ces premières années en tant qu’a: During those first years as a community development officer, Kemba also joined the school’s equity, diversity and inclusion working group. “We worked for about a year to draft recommendations for the school board, which approved them. But so far they haven’t been implemented in schools,” she says, visibly irritated. The reason for the delay? She doesn’t know.
Face à ce qu’elle considère comme un man: Faced with what she considers a lack of responsiveness, she takes matters into her own hands and launches her own anti-Black racism strategy consulting, alongside her community officer job. “I launched this initiative in response to needs I had observed,” she insists, determined.
Aujourd’hui, Kemba est invitée de manièr: Today, Kemba is regularly invited to schools across Greater Montréal for these interventions. “I’m often called after verbally violent incidents in schools. So far, word of mouth has been very effective,” she tells us proudly.
<strong>L’approche antiraciste : un moye: The anti-racist approach: a way to educate students and teachers
Daniel*, qui est d’origine latino-québéc: Daniel*, who is of Latino-Quebecer background, is a history, geography, and ethics and religious culture teacher in Côte Saint-Luc. At his high school, the racialized teachers are numerous and diverse. Yet he observes disparities in how Black students are treated.
« Ce que je constate, c’est que, si tu e: “What I see is that if you’re Black, you’ll have more problems at school for various reasons, because we operate in a mostly white system. A white Quebecer student really has to do a lot, unlike a Black student, to be suspended or expelled, for example. There are a lot of unconscious biases, and even though I’m mixed myself, I’ve had some prejudices too,” he admits.
Malgré huit ans d’expérience en tant que: Despite eight years of experience as a teacher in several schools, Daniel admits he has never received training on the EDI approach. “It’s kind of a jungle; every teacher is left to fend for themselves when it comes to EDI. Everyone talks about it however they want… or not,” he says. Then he continues: “There’s no follow-up, nobody checks whether the concepts discussed at the beginning of the year were put into practice or not.”
« Honnêtement, je ne sais pas si la prio: “Honestly, I don’t know if the priority in education right now is to do training on that. We’re more focused on entrance grades, absences, intervention plans, but when it comes to Equity, Diversity, Inclusion, it’s still waiting…”
Alors, pour aborder la question du racis: So, to address the question of racism, Daniel relies on his personal knowledge as well as his experiences. “I’m mixed, so it’s easier to teach when you know a bit about diversity, but that’s not the case for everyone,” the teacher acknowledges.
Selon lui, une formation sur l’antiracis: In his view, anti-racism training would be welcome in schools: “A lot of teachers struggle to talk about taboo subjects, for fear of being judged or not being understood, or of being misinterpreted. Students, whether they experience racism or commit it, know that racism is everywhere. They just don’t know how to explain it, see it or understand it. Sometimes racism is trivialized, sometimes it’s blatant. Some clarification would help them.”
Bien que la diversité soit désormais bie: Although diversity is now firmly rooted in the school landscape of some Montréal neighbourhoods, Daniel believes school is still not a place of inclusion. For him, the issue of racism in the education system isn’t limited to the attitude of some teachers, but extends to school curricula as well.
<strong>« C’est clairement l’histoire bl: “It’s clearly white history that we’re teaching”
Dès septembre, le cours d’Éthique et de: Starting in September, the Ethics and Religious Culture course will be replaced by a new program called <l1>Quebec Culture and Citizenship</l1>, a title that quietly makes the teacher laugh. “This course will remove religion from the curriculum. But in a context where there are a lot of immigrants, that simply goes against inclusion. Here, the goal is only to strengthen Quebec identity,” he says. “But generally speaking, I could say that the history or geography curriculum is racist, because it’s clearly white history that we’re teaching.”
Kemba Mitchell est du même avis. « Les e: Kemba Mitchell shares this view. “Teachers aren’t spreading hate, but courses that emphasize Europe send the message to people who don’t fit the European profile that they aren’t important or included – and that has repercussions on their self-esteem. Which also explains why Black students fail more often than others,” she says with a sigh. Then she continues: “And if they have certain aspirations, educators’ implicit biases can steer them in another direction.”
<strong>Des ateliers par les Noirs, pour: Workshops by Black people, for Black people, for everyone’s equity
Cette observation a notamment poussé la: This observation notably led the Black anti-racism consultant to offer webinars to Black students, whom she considers less informed than the rest of the students. “It’s not that certain information isn’t communicated to them, but they’re less informed about future prospects because, often unconsciously, they don’t feel concerned. Either because they haven’t had role models, or because they’ve been reduced to something else.”
Parmi les consultations que propose Kemb: Among the consultations Kemba offers, some webinars are provided free of charge to the Black community to “fill certain gaps in the education system,” she explains. Among other things, she organizes webinars on scholarships.
« Je sais qu’il y a des conseillers d’or: “I know there are guidance counsellors, but they kind of just say: ‘Here are our scholarships, apply.’ But because of what goes on in schools, Black students often don’t feel concerned. They don’t even book appointments with guidance counsellors. Whether it’s because they think they can’t get these scholarships or because they find it too much work, these students each have their reasons for not even trying. But not trying is unacceptable,” she says sharply.
Elle rappelle que les bourses ne sont pa: She points out that scholarships aren’t only financial support but also a springboard to broader opportunities: “Some offer opportunities to travel abroad or to another province. They can provide chances to network with different companies or communities. So it’s not just about money, it’s also an opportunity to write truly creative and unique cover letters.”
La consultante se concentre également su: The consultant also focuses on other practical aspects, such as writing a good résumé and building relationships with teachers. “An essential step for getting references,” she stresses.
Dans ses consultations en stratégie anti: Through her anti-racist strategy consultations and her webinars, Kemba Mitchell strives to fill the gap in resources and support faced by Black students in Montréal. An initiative that is gradually gaining popularity. “This fall, several schools want me to come back, and new ones are already asking me to visit,” she tells us proudly before we part ways.
